scorecard.rationale: Two independent placebo-controlled menopause trials report less joint and muscular discomfort with oral Salvia officinalis fresh-tip extract (n=48 per-protocol of 80, p<.05) and dry extract (n=59, p<.001 with reversed table statistics), supported by a dose-comparison sage leaf throat-spray trial (n=164, p=.0021) and preclinical antinociception. Competing safety signals include one excessive-intake abdominal pain case (6/10) and a non-significant adverse-event count in an Alzheimer dry-extract trial (2 vs 0, p=.23), while perioperative/cancer rinse and mixed-herb trials give no isolated oral pain effect. Because no study evaluates fresh culinary sage or Parkinson pain severity, the controlled non-Parkinson discomfort reductions sustain only a minimal_signal against worsening. The additional screen confirms a distinct Salvia officinalis leaf extract entry and distinguishes white sage. Its biochemical response supplies no pain direction and leaves the existing minimal easing lean unchanged. The ursolic acid review names common sage and describes isolated-compound analgesic experiments. No fresh-sage intervention or compound concentration in culinary use links it to the pain comparison.
